title: Proposition

\label{prop:intro}

title: Remark
body_md:
In the final stages of preparing this paper, the author was made aware of related work by Nechitailo \cite{Nechitailo} that also found a $3$-color relation in type $H_3$.
                The approaches between the two papers differ substantially with the main similarity being the use of polynomial interpolation.
                In particular, \emph{loc. cit.} solves for the coefficients by computing inverses of blocks of localization matrices evaluating at a fixed point whereas our approach uses forward-substitution using the $\lambda$-functionals
                developed in this paper.

                Nechitailo's relation involved 43,424 nonzero coefficients, and is not further simplified. The better efficiency of the algorithm in the present work made it quite feasible
                to check all possible $3$-color relations for a fixed choice of light-leaf datum. This allowed us to find a minimal relation with 125 nonzero coefficients, and then further simplify it using thick Soergel calculus.
                
                Finally, the code accompanying \emph{loc. cit.} is specialized to $H_3$ and cannot be used to find double-leaf expansions for more general morphisms or Coxeter groups.
                The code accompanying this paper was designed to be a general-purpose Soergel calculus utility.
                However, our code is implemented in Python which tends to be much slower than a modern performant language like Rust used in Nechitailo's implementation.
                A port of the codebase for this paper to a language like Rust would likely yield even higher efficiency gains.

title: Proof
body_md:
By \cite[Theorem 3.8]{Hazi1}, one has that \eqref{eq:qbinom_vanishing} holds if and only if $\Psi_m (a_{st} a_{ts}) = 0$.
                This is also stated explicitly in \cite[(15)]{Hazi1}. 
                If $m$ is even, the balancedness equation \eqref{eq:balanced} is automatic under \eqref{eq:qbinom_vanishing} as observed in \cite[Lemma 6.25]{EWloc}.
                As a result, we only need to consider the case of $m$ being odd.

                Assume that $m$ is odd, and that both \eqref{eq:qbinom_vanishing} and \eqref{eq:balanced} hold. 
                By \cite[Theorem 2.3]{Hazi2}, the element $a_{st} a_{ts}$ has a square root $a$ in $\mathbbm{k}^{\times}$.
                Moreover, this element satisfies $\Psi_m' (a) = 0$ and 
                \[[m-1]_x (-a_{st}, -a_{ts}) = \frac{-a_{st}}{a} \qquad\text{and}\qquad [m-1]_y (-a_{st}, -a_{ts}) = \frac{-a_{ts}}{a}.\]
                Balancedness \eqref{eq:balanced} then forces $a_{st} = a_{ts} = -a$, and therefore $\Psi_m' (-a_{st}) = 0$.

                Conversely, suppose that $a_{st} = a_{ts}$ and $\Psi_m' (-a_{st}) = 0$. 
                Since $2 \cos (\pi/m)$ is a root of $\Psi_m (z^2)$, its monic minimal polynomial $\Psi_m' (z)$ divides $\Psi_m (z^2)$ in $\mathbb{Z} [z]$.
                As a result, $\Psi_m (a_{st} a_{ts}) = \Psi_m (a_{st}^2) = 0$. By\cite[Theorem 3.8]{Hazi1}, the quantum-binomial vanishing condition holds. 
                Now apply \cite[Corollary 2.5]{Hazi2} to conclude balancedness.

\label{ex:golden_realization}
                The most prominent realization we will encounter in this paper is the \emph{golden realization}.
                Let $(W,S)$ be a Coxeter system for which $m_{st} \in \{2,3,5,\infty\}$. Set $\mathbbm{k} = \mathbb{Q} (\phi)$ where $\phi = (1 + \sqrt{5})/2$ denotes the golden ratio.
                Note that $\mathbbm{k}$ is isomorphic to the field of fractions for $\mathbb{Z} [\tau]/(\tau^2 - \tau - 1)$ via $\tau \mapsto \phi$.
                We set $\mathfrak{h} = \bigoplus_{s \in S} \mathbbm{k} \alpha_s^{\vee}$ and define $\alpha_s \in \mathfrak{h}^*$ via
                \[\langle \alpha_s^{\vee} , \alpha_t \rangle = \begin{cases} 2 & \text{if }s=t, \\ 0 & \text{if }m_{st} = 2, \\ -1 & \text{if }m_{st} = 3, \\ -\phi & \text{if } m_{st} = 5, \\ -2 & \text{if } m_{st} = \infty.\end{cases}\] 
                It is easy to check from its definition that $\mathfrak{h}$ is always a balanced realization.

label: lem:detecting_bimodularity
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:detecting_bimodularity}
                Let $M, N \in \mathsf{C} (\mathfrak{h}, W)$ such that $M$ and $N$ are finitely generated as $R$-bimodules and flat as right $R$-modules.
                Let $\varphi : M \to N$ be a left $R$-module map. Assume that there are left $R$-module maps $\varphi^w : M^w \to N^w$ satisfying
                \[\pi_N^w \circ \varphi = \varphi^w \circ \pi_M^w\]
                for all $w \in W$.
                Then $\varphi$ is a morphism in $\mathsf{C} (\mathfrak{h}, W)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We can first show that $\varphi$ is a morphism of $R$-bimodules.
                Let $m \in M$ and $r \in R$. For all $w \in W$, one has that
                \[\pi_N^w (\varphi (mr) - \varphi (m) r) = \varphi^w (w(r) \pi_M^w (m)) - w(r) \varphi^w (\pi_M^w (m)) = 0.\]
                By \eqref{eq:Mw_and_embedding}, we deduce that $\varphi (mr) = \varphi (m) r$, and so $\varphi$ is a morphism of $R$-bimodules.

                It remains to check that $\varphi$ preserves the localization data. By \cite[Lemma 2.4]{Abe19}, $M^w \otimes_R Q = M_Q^w$ and $N^w \otimes_R Q = N_Q^w$.
                The twisted right actions show that each $\varphi^w$ is also right $R$-linear. Localizing the identities $\pi_N^w \varphi = \varphi^w \pi_M^w$ then shows that $\varphi_Q$ acts componentwise by $\varphi^w \otimes_R Q$.
                Therefore, $\varphi_Q (M_Q^w) \subseteq N_Q^w$ as desired.

title: Definition
body_md:
Let $(\mathfrak{h}, \{\alpha_s\}_{s \in S}, \{\alpha_s^{\vee}\}_{s \in S})$ be a realization of $W$ over $\mathbbm{k}$ and $(\mathfrak{h}', \{\alpha_s'\}_{s \in S}, \{(\alpha_s')^{\vee}\}_{s \in S})$ be a realization of $W$ over $\mathbbm{k}'$. 
        A \emph{morphism of realizations} $\mathfrak{h} \to \mathfrak{h}'$ consists of a pair $(\sigma, f)$ where $\sigma : \mathbbm{k} \to \mathbbm{k}'$ is a ring homomorphism and $f : \mathfrak{h}^* \to (\mathfrak{h}')^*$ is a $\mathbbm{k}$-linear map via $\sigma$ 
        such that for all $s \in S$  and $v \in \mathfrak{h}^*$, 
        \[f ( \alpha_s ) = \alpha_s' \qquad\text{and}\qquad \langle (\alpha_s')^{\vee}, f (v) \rangle = \sigma (\langle \alpha_s^{\vee}, v \rangle).\]

title: Remark
body_md:
It would be more natural to view a realization as the space $\mathfrak{h}^*$ rather than $\mathfrak{h}$ in the above definition so that a morphism of realizations
                arises via a linear map on the ambient spaces rather than their duals.
                This convention on realizations is used, for example, in \cite{Abe19}.

label: lem:real_and_demazure
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:real_and_demazure}
        Let $(\sigma, f) : \mathfrak{h} \to \mathfrak{h}'$ be a morphism of realizations. Then
        \[f \circ \partial_s^{\mathfrak{h}} = \partial_s^{\mathfrak{h}'} \circ f.\]
        As a result, if $\delta_s \in \mathfrak{h}^*$ satisfies $\partial_s^{\mathfrak{h}} (\delta_s) = 1$, then for $\delta_s' \coloneq f (\delta_s)$, one has that $\partial_s^{\mathfrak{h}'} (\delta_s') = 1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $r \in R_{\mathfrak{h}}$ and $s \in S$. Then
        \[\alpha_s' f (\partial_s^{\mathfrak{h}} (r)) = f (\alpha_s \partial_s^{\mathfrak{h}} (r)) = f(r - s(r)) = f(r) - s f(r) = \alpha_s' \partial_s^{\mathfrak{h}'} f(r).\]
        Since $R_{\mathfrak{h}'}$ is an integral domain, we conclude that the Demazure operators commute with $f$.
        As a result, $\partial_s^{\mathfrak{h}'} (\delta_s') = f (\partial_s^{\mathfrak{h}} (\delta_s)) = 1$.

label: lem:Bs_left_module_isom
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:Bs_left_module_isom}
                Let $\underline{w} = (s_1, \ldots, s_k)$ be an expression in $W$. The map 
                \[
                \jmath_{\underline{w}} : B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathfrak{h}} \to B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathfrak{h}'}, \qquad r_1 \otimes \ldots \otimes r_{k+1} \mapsto f (r_1) \otimes \ldots \otimes f (r_{k+1}) 
                \]
                is well-defined and $R_{\mathfrak{h}}$-linear. Moreover, the induced map 
                \[\iota_{\underline{w}} : R_{\mathfrak{h}'} \otimes_{R_{\mathfrak{h}}} B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathfrak{h}} \to B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathfrak{h}'}\]
                is an isomorphism of graded left $R_{\mathfrak{h}'}$-modules.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The fact that $\jmath_{\underline{w}}$ is well-defined follows from $f$ being $W$-equivariant, and so, $f (R_{\mathfrak{h}}^s) \subseteq R_{\mathfrak{h}'}^s$.

                From the discussion preceding the lemma, the collection of elements $\{ 1 \otimes t_{\underline{w}, \mathbf{e}}^{\mathfrak{h}} \}_{\mathbf{e} \in \operatorname{Sub} (\underline{w})}$ (resp. $\{ t_{\underline{w}, \mathbf{e}}^{\mathfrak{h}'} \}_{\mathbf{e} \in \operatorname{Sub} (\underline{w})}$)
                forms a left $R_{\mathfrak{h}'}$-basis for $R_{\mathfrak{h}'} \otimes_{R_{\mathfrak{h}}} B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathfrak{h}}$ (resp. $B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathfrak{h'}}$).
                It follows from its construction that $\iota_{\underline{w}} (1 \otimes t_{\underline{w}, \mathbf{e}}^{\mathfrak{h}}) = t_{\underline{w}, \mathbf{e}}^{\mathfrak{h}'}$ for all $\mathbf{e} \in \operatorname{Sub} (\underline{w})$. As a result, $\iota_{\underline{w}}$ is an isomorphism of left $R_{\mathfrak{h}'}$-modules.

label: lem:Bs_w_left_module_isom
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:Bs_w_left_module_isom}
                Let $\underline{w} = (s_1, \ldots, s_k)$ be an expression in $W$ and $x \in W$. 
                There is a left $R_{\mathfrak{h}}$-linear map
                \[
                \jmath_{\underline{w}}^x : B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathfrak{h}, x} \to B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathfrak{h}', x} 
                \]
                such that 
                \[\jmath_{\underline{w}}^x \circ \pi_{B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathfrak{h}}}^x = \pi_{B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathfrak{h}'}}^x \circ \jmath_{\underline{w}}. \]
                 Moreover, the induced map 
                \[\iota_{\underline{w}}^x : R_{\mathfrak{h}'} \otimes_{R_{\mathfrak{h}}} B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathfrak{h}, x} \to B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathfrak{h}', x}\]
                is an isomorphism of graded left $R_{\mathfrak{h}'}$-modules.
head: environment

label: eq:Bs_w_left_module_isom_1
title: Proof
body_md:
The map $\jmath_{\underline{w}} : B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathfrak{h}} \to B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathfrak{h}'}$ induces a $Q_{\mathfrak{h}}$-linear map
                \[\jmath_{\underline{w}, Q} : B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathfrak{h}} \otimes_{R_{\mathfrak{h}}} Q_{\mathfrak{h}} \to B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathfrak{h}'} \otimes_{R_{\mathfrak{h}'}} Q_{\mathfrak{h}'}, \qquad m \otimes q \mapsto \jmath_{\underline{w}} (m) \otimes f_Q (q).\]
                We claim that $\jmath_{\underline{w}, Q}$ takes $x$-components to $x$-components.
                Recall from Lemma~\ref{lem:decomp_into_loc_pieces}, that there is a decomposition of $Q_{\mathfrak{h}}$-modules
                \[(B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathfrak{h}})_Q^x = \bigoplus_{\underline{w}^{\mathbf{e}} = x} q_{\underline{w}}^{\mathbf{e}, \mathfrak{h}} Q_{\mathfrak{h}},\]
                where $q_{\underline{w}}^{\mathbf{e}, \mathfrak{h}}$ is defined as in \eqref{eq:qwe}. It is clear that $\jmath_{\underline{w}, Q} (q_{\underline{w}}^{\mathbf{e}, \mathfrak{h}}) = q_{\underline{w}}^{\mathbf{e}, \mathfrak{h}'}$.
                As a result, 
                \[ \jmath_{\underline{w}, Q} ((B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathfrak{h}})_Q^x ) \subseteq (B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathfrak{h}'})_Q^x\]
                for all $x \in W$. The formula
                \begin{equation}\label{eq:Bs_w_left_module_isom_1}
                        \jmath_{\underline{w}}^x (\pi_{B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathfrak{h}}}^x (m) ) = \pi_{B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathfrak{h}'}}^x (\jmath_{\underline{w}} (m)) 
                \end{equation}
                then defines a left $R_{\mathfrak{h}}$-linear map
                \[\jmath_{\underline{w}}^x : B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathfrak{h}, x} \to B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathfrak{h}', x}.\]
                This map induces a left $R_{\mathfrak{h}'}$-linear map
                \[\iota_{\underline{w}}^x : R_{\mathfrak{h}'} \otimes_{R_{\mathfrak{h}}} B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathfrak{h}, x} \to B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathfrak{h}', x}.\]
                
                It remains to show that $\iota_{\underline{w}}^x$ is an isomorphism of graded left $R_{\mathfrak{h}'}$-modules.
                By Proposition~\ref{prop:bases_of_BS}, the sets $\{ 1 \otimes b_{\underline{w}, \mathbf{e}}^{\mathfrak{h}, x} \}_{\mathbf{e} \in \operatorname{Sub}^x (\underline{w})} \subset R_{\mathfrak{h}'} \otimes_{R_{\mathfrak{h}}} B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathfrak{h}, x}$ and $\{ b_{\underline{w}, \mathbf{e}}^{\mathfrak{h}', x} \}_{\mathbf{e} \in \operatorname{Sub}^x (\underline{w})} \subset B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathfrak{h}', x}$
                are left $R_{\mathfrak{h}'}$-module bases.
                Moreover, it can be easily checked from the definitions and \eqref{eq:Bs_w_left_module_isom_1} that the basis for $R_{\mathfrak{h}'} \otimes_{R_{\mathfrak{h}}} B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathfrak{h}, x}$ is sent to the basis for $B_{\underline{w}}^{\mathfrak{h}' , x}$.
                As a result, $\iota_{\underline{w}}^x$ is an isomorphism of graded left $R_{\mathfrak{h}'}$-modules.

label: prop:BS_functor
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:BS_functor}
        Let $\varphi : B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathfrak{h}} \to B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathfrak{h}}$.
        The map $\mathsf{ABS}_f (\varphi) : B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathfrak{h}'} \to B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathfrak{h}'}$ is a morphism of Abe--Bott--Samelson bimodules. This defines a monoidal functor
        \[\mathsf{ABS}_f : \mathsf{ABS} (\mathfrak{h}, W) \to \mathsf{ABS} (\mathfrak{h}', W).\]

title: Proof
body_md:
Set $\psi = \mathsf{ABS}_f (\varphi)$ and $\psi^w = \mathsf{ABS}_f^w (\varphi)$.
                By Lemma~\ref{lem:Bs_w_left_module_isom}, one has that
                \[\pi_{B_{\underline{y}}^{\mathfrak{h}'}}^w \circ \psi = \psi^w \circ \pi_{B_{\underline{x}}^{\mathfrak{h}'}}^w \]
                for all $w \in W$.
                It follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:detecting_bimodularity} that $\psi$ is a morphism of Abe--Bott--Samelson bimodules.

                The functorality and monoidality of $\mathsf{ABS}_f$ is a routine check and omitted.

label: prop:behavior_of_BS_on_generators
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:behavior_of_BS_on_generators}
                \begin{enumerate}
                        \item Let $s \in S$. Recall the one-color maps,
                        \[\nu_{\mathfrak{h}}^s : B_s \to B_s \otimes B_s, \qquad \epsilon_{\mathfrak{h}}^s : B_s \to R, \qquad \mu_{\mathfrak{h}}^s : B_s \otimes_R B_s \to B_s, \qquad \eta_{\mathfrak{h}}^s : R \to B_s . \]
                        Under $\mathsf{ABS}_f$, one has that
                        \[\mathsf{ABS}_f (\nu_{\mathfrak{h}}^s) = \nu_{\mathfrak{h}'}^s, \qquad \mathsf{ABS}_f (\epsilon_{\mathfrak{h}}^s) = \epsilon_{\mathfrak{h}'}^s, \qquad \mathsf{ABS}_f (\mu_{\mathfrak{h}}^s) = \mu_{\mathfrak{h}'}^s, \qquad \mathsf{ABS}_f (\eta_{\mathfrak{h}}^s) = \eta_{\mathfrak{h}'}^s.\]
                        \item Let $s,t \in S$ be distinct simple reflections with $m_{st} < \infty$. Recall the braid morphism
                        \[\beta_{st}^{\mathfrak{h}} : B_{{}_s \underline{m}}^{\mathfrak{h}} \to B_{{}_t \underline{m}}^{\mathfrak{h}}.\]
                        We have that
                        \[\mathsf{ABS}_f (\beta_{st}^{\mathfrak{h}}) = \beta_{st}^{\mathfrak{h}'}.\]
                        \item For a fixed common $\operatorname{LL}$-datum, $\mathsf{ABS}_f$ sends each light leaf and double leaf to the corresponding one for $\mathfrak{h}'$. In particular, it identifies the indexed double-leaf bases.
                \end{enumerate}

title: Proof
body_md:
Statement (1) can be easily checked from the definitions of these morphisms using Lemma~\ref{lem:real_and_demazure} and the definition of $\mathsf{ABS}_f$.
        For (2), the uniqueness of $\beta_{st}$ reduces the work to checking that $\mathsf{ABS}_f (\beta_{st}^{\mathfrak{h}})$ takes $1$-tensors to $1$-tensors.
        However, $\mathsf{ABS}_f$ is defined by $f$ on each tensor factor, so this is clear as well.
        Finally, (3) is an immediate consequence of (1) and (2).

title: Corollary

title: Proof
body_md:
We will just prove the first statement as the second follows from the same argument.
                If  $f : R_\mathfrak{h} \to R_{\mathfrak{h}'}$ is injective, then Theorem~\ref{thm:dll_basis} and Proposition~\ref{prop:behavior_of_BS_on_generators} (3) together imply that $\mathsf{ABS}_f$ is faithful.

label: eq:dagger_and_product_1
title: Proof
body_md:
The definition of $\zeta$ gives
        \[\zeta_{\underline{x} \underline{x}'} (\mathbf{e} \mathbf{e}') = \zeta_{\underline{x}} (\mathbf{e}) \underline{x}^{\mathbf{e}} (\zeta_{\underline{x}'} (\mathbf{e}')).\]
        We can use this with definition of $\star$ from \eqref{eq:tensor_prod_of_Q_mats} to compute
        \begin{equation}\label{eq:dagger_and_product_1}
                (A \star B)_{\mathbf{e} \mathbf{e}', \mathbf{f} \mathbf{f}'}^{\dagger} = \frac{\zeta_{\underline{y}} (\mathbf{f}) \underline{y}^{\mathbf{f}} (\zeta_{\underline{y}'} (\mathbf{f}'))}{\zeta_{\underline{x}} (\mathbf{e}) \underline{x}^{\mathbf{e}} (\zeta_{\underline{x}'} (\mathbf{e}'))} A_{\mathbf{f}, \mathbf{e}} \underline{x}^{\mathbf{e}} (B_{\mathbf{f}', \mathbf{e}'}).
        \end{equation}
        If $A_{\mathbf{f}, \mathbf{e}} = 0$, then right-hand side vanishes and there is nothing to show. 
        If $A_{\mathbf{f}, \mathbf{e}} \neq 0$, then we must have that $\underline{x}^{\mathbf{e}} = w = \underline{y}^{\mathbf{f}}$. 
        As a result \eqref{eq:dagger_and_product_1} becomes
        \begin{align*}
                 (A \star B)_{\mathbf{e} \mathbf{e}', \mathbf{f} \mathbf{f}'}^{\dagger} &= \left( \frac{\zeta_{\underline{y}} (\mathbf{f})}{\zeta_{\underline{x}} (\mathbf{e})} A_{\mathbf{f}, \mathbf{e}} \right) w \left( \frac{\zeta_{\underline{y}'} (\mathbf{f}') }{\zeta_{\underline{x}'} (\mathbf{e}')} B_{\mathbf{f}', \mathbf{e}'}\right) \\
                 &= A_{\mathbf{e}, \mathbf{f}}^{\dagger} \underline{y}^{\mathbf{f}} (B_{\mathbf{e}', \mathbf{f}'}^{\dagger}) \\
                 &= (A^{\dagger} \star B^{\dagger})_{\mathbf{e} \mathbf{e}', \mathbf{f} \mathbf{f}'}.
        \end{align*}

label: eq:big_eqn_system
title: Goal
body_md:
Let $W$ be a finite rank-3 Coxeter group. Let $w_0$ be the longest element in $W$ and pick two reduced expressions $\underline{x}$ and $\underline{y}$ for $w_0$.
                Let $p$ and $q$ be distinct paths in the rex graph of $w_0$ from $\underline{x}$ to $\underline{y}$ around a Zamolodchikov cycle.
                There are corresponding morphisms $\beta_p$ and $\beta_q$ from $B_{\underline{x}}$ to $B_{\underline{y}}$ in $\mathsf{ABS} (\mathfrak{h}, W)$. 
                To complete the definition of the Elias--Williamson category, one needs to find a linear combination of double leaves
                \[\beta_p - \beta_q = \sum_{\underline{x}^\mathbf{e} = w = \underline{y}^\mathbf{f}} c_{\mathbf{e}, \mathbf{f}}^w \mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_{\mathbf{e}, \mathbf{f}}.\]
                In light of the localization functor, it suffices to solve the enormous matrix equations
                \begin{equation}\label{eq:big_eqn_system}
                        \Lambda (\beta_p - \beta_q) =  \sum_{\underline{x}^\mathbf{e} = w = \underline{y}^\mathbf{f}} c_{\mathbf{e}, \mathbf{f}}^w \Lambda (\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_{\mathbf{e}, \mathbf{f}}).
                \end{equation}
                When $W$ is of type $A_3$ or type $B_3$, the saving grace is that the $c_{\mathbf{e}, \mathbf{f}}^w = 0$ for all subexpressions provided one chooses $\underline{x}$ and $\underline{y}$ in a clever manner.
                For type $A_1 \times I_2 (m)$, one again has that $c_{\mathbf{e}, \mathbf{f}}^w = 0$; however, one can show this directly without localization.

                The hard case, and the subject of the paper, is handling the type $H_3$ case. It was already calculated by Elias--Williamson that no choice of rexes will cause the coefficients $c_{\mathbf{e}, \mathbf{f}}^w$ to be all $0$.
                Proceeding naively, even writing down this system of equations would involve the multiplication of many sparse matrices with $2^{15} = 32768$ rows.
                Computing the localization matrices is still doable with some effort (although in practice you never multiply these massive sparse matrices).
                However, solving the system of equations efficiently requires some new insight.

label: lem:column_of_loc_matrix_for_LL
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:column_of_loc_matrix_for_LL}
                If a column $\mathbf{c}$ of $\Lambda (\operatorname{LL}_{\underline{x}, \mathbf{e}})$ is nonzero, then $\mathbf{c} \leq \mathbf{e}$.
head: environment

label: eq:column_of_loc_matrix_for_LL_1
title: Proof
body_md:
Write $\underline{x} = (s_1, \ldots, s_k)$ and set $\underline{w} = \operatorname{rex} (\underline{x}^{\mathbf{e}})$.
                Assume that $\Lambda (\operatorname{LL}_{\underline{x}, \mathbf{e}})_{\bullet, \mathbf{c}} \neq 0$. By the definition of the path dominance order, we need to show that $\underline{x}_i^{\mathbf{c}} \leq \underline{x}_i^{\mathbf{e}}$ for all $i=1,\ldots, k$. 
                Fix $i \in \{1, \ldots, k \}$ and let $\underline{r}_i$ be the reduced expression for $\underline{x}_i^{\mathbf{e}}$ occurring after the $i$-th step of the light-leaf construction. Recall the map $\operatorname{LL}_{\underline{x}, \mathbf{e}}^i : B_{\underline{x}} \to B_{\underline{r}_i s_{i+1} \ldots s_k}$.
                By construction, we can write 
                \begin{equation}\label{eq:column_of_loc_matrix_for_LL_1}
                        \operatorname{LL}_{\underline{x}, \mathbf{e}}^i = F_i \otimes \operatorname{id}_{B_{(s_{i+1}, \ldots, s_k)}}
                \end{equation}
                where $F_i : B_{(s_1, \ldots, s_i)} \to B_{\underline{r}_i}$. Now write $\operatorname{LL}_{\underline{x}, \mathbf{e}} = G_i \circ \operatorname{LL}_{\underline{x}, \mathbf{e}}^i$ where $G_i : B_{\underline{r}_i s_{i+1} \ldots s_k} \to B_{\underline{w}}$ is the morphism obtained by finishing the light leaf construction.
                By functorality of localization, we have that $\Lambda (\operatorname{LL}_{\underline{x}, \mathbf{e}}) = \Lambda (G_i) \Lambda (\operatorname{LL}_{\underline{x}, \mathbf{e}}^i)$.
                Since the column $\mathbf{c}$ of $\Lambda (\operatorname{LL}_{\underline{x}, \mathbf{e}})$ is nonzero, elementary linear algebra says that the column $\mathbf{c}$ of $\Lambda (\operatorname{LL}_{\underline{x}, \mathbf{e}}^i)$ is nonzero.
                By Lemma~\ref{lem:prod_of_loc_mats}, the tensor product decomposition of \eqref{eq:column_of_loc_matrix_for_LL_1} implies that the column $\mathbf{c}_{\leq i}$ of $\Lambda (F_i)$ is nonzero.
                In particular, we can find a subexpression $\mathbf{h}$ of $\underline{r}_i$ such that $\Lambda (F_i)_{\mathbf{h}, \mathbf{c}_{\leq i}} \neq 0$, and hence, $\underline{x}_i^{\mathbf{c}} = \underline{r}_i^{\mathbf{h}}$.
                Since $\underline{r}_i$ is a reduced expression for $\underline{x}_i^{\mathbf{e}}$, we must have that $\underline{r}_i^{\mathbf{h}} \leq \underline{x}_i^{\mathbf{e}}$, and so $\underline{x}_i^{\mathbf{c}} \leq \underline{x}_i^{\mathbf{e}}$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
Lemma~\ref{lem:column_of_loc_matrix_for_LL} can be thought of as a mild generalization of path dominance upper-triangularity for light leaves (see \cite[Proposition 6.6]{EW}).
                In particular, if $\mathbf{c}$ is a subexpression of $\underline{x}$, then path dominance upper-triangularity says that if $\Lambda (\operatorname{LL}_{\underline{x}, \mathbf{e}})_{\mathbf{1}, \mathbf{c}} \neq 0$, then $\mathbf{c} \leq \mathbf{e}$.

label: thm:lower_triang_of_coord_functionals
title: Theorem
head: environment

label: eq:lower_triang_of_coord_functionals_1
title: Proof
body_md:
Assume that $\lambda_i (\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_j) \neq 0$.
                 By Proposition~\ref{prop:loc_of_dl}, one has that 
                \begin{equation}\label{eq:lower_triang_of_coord_functionals_1}
                        \lambda_i (\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_j) = \frac{1}{\zeta_{\underline{y}} (\mathbf{f}^i)} \sum_{\mathbf{h} \in \operatorname{Sub} (\operatorname{rex} (w_j))} \zeta_{\operatorname{rex} (w_j)} (\mathbf{h}) (\Lambda (\operatorname{LL}_{\underline{y}, \mathbf{f}^j})_{\mathbf{h}, \mathbf{f}^i} ) (\Lambda (\operatorname{LL}_{\underline{x}, \mathbf{e}^j})_{\mathbf{h}, \mathbf{e}^i} ).
                \end{equation}
                If \eqref{eq:lower_triang_of_coord_functionals_1} is nonzero, then Lemma~\ref{lem:column_of_loc_matrix_for_LL} implies that $\mathbf{e}^i \leq \mathbf{e}^j$ and $\mathbf{f}^i \leq \mathbf{f}^j$.
                In particular, $w_i = \underline{x}^{\mathbf{e}^i} \leq \underline{x}^{\mathbf{e}^j} = w_j$. If $w_i \neq w_j$, then $\ell (w_i) < \ell (w_j)$, and so $j \leq i$.
                If $w_i = w_j$ but $i \neq j$, then either $\mathbf{e}^i \neq \mathbf{e}^j$ or $\mathbf{f}^i \neq \mathbf{f}^j$. 
                In particular, $h_{\underline{x}} (\mathbf{e}^i) + h_{\underline{y}} (\mathbf{f}^i) < h_{\underline{x}} (\mathbf{e}^j) + h_{\underline{y}} (\mathbf{f}^j)$, and so $j \leq i$.


               We will now consider $\lambda_i (\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_i)$.
                For $\Lambda (\operatorname{LL}_{\underline{x}, \mathbf{e}^i})_{\mathbf{h}, \mathbf{e}^i} \neq 0$, we must have that $\operatorname{rex} (w_i)^{\mathbf{h}} = \underline{x}^{\mathbf{e}^i} = w_i$. This can only happen when $\mathbf{h} = \mathbf{1}$.
                As a result, \eqref{eq:lower_triang_of_coord_functionals_1} simplifies to
                \begin{align*}
                        \lambda_i (\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_i) &= \frac{\zeta_{\operatorname{rex} (w_i)} (\mathbf{1})}{\zeta_{\underline{y}} (\mathbf{f}^i)}  (\Lambda (\operatorname{LL}_{\underline{y}, \mathbf{f}^i})_{\mathbf{1}, \mathbf{f}^i}) (\Lambda (\operatorname{LL}_{\underline{x}, \mathbf{e}^i})_{\mathbf{1}, \mathbf{e}^i}) \\
                        &= \frac{\zeta_{\operatorname{rex} (w_i)} (\mathbf{1})}{\zeta_{\underline{y}} (\mathbf{f}^i)} \gamma_{\underline{x}} (\mathbf{e}^i) \gamma_{\underline{y}} (\mathbf{f}^i),
                \end{align*}
                where the second equality follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:coeff_of_LL_at_e}.
                Note that all factors in \eqref{eq:lower_triang_of_coord_functionals_0} are roots or products of roots. In particular, their inverses exist in $Q$, and so, \eqref{eq:lower_triang_of_coord_functionals_0} is invertible in $Q$.

title: Remark
body_md:
The utility of Corollary~\ref{cor:recursion_for_coeffs} is that it gives a recursive algorithm for finding the coefficients appearing in a double leaves expansion.
                More precisely, the lower triangularity of Theorem~\ref{thm:lower_triang_of_coord_functionals} allows one to perform an efficient forward substitution of the system of equations
                \[\Lambda (\varphi) = \sum_{i=1}^N c_i \Lambda (\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_i).\]

                After these localization coefficients are computed, determining the $c_i$'s amounts to simple forward substitution. For example,
                \begin{align*}
                        c_1 &= \frac{\lambda_1 (\varphi)}{\lambda_1 (\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_1)} \\
                        c_2 &= \frac{\lambda_2 (\varphi) - c_1 \lambda_2 (\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_1)}{\lambda_2 (\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_2)} \\
                        c_3 &=  \frac{\lambda_3 (\varphi) - c_1 \lambda_3 (\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_1) - c_2 \lambda_3 (\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_2)}{\lambda_3 (\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_3)}.
                \end{align*}

\label{rem:generic_to_degree_d}

            Let $\varphi : B_{\underline{x}} \to B_{\underline{y}}$ be a degree $d$ morphism.
            For each $i=1,\ldots, N$, set $d_i$ to be the degree of $\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_i$. We can consider the set

label: prop:interpolation
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By \eqref{eq:leading_term_of_binom_poly}, the set $\{ B_{a}^{\tilde{a}} \}_{a \in L_d}$ is a basis for $A_n^{\leq d}$.
                Moreover, under the standard basis of $A_n^{\leq d}$ by monomials ordered under the graded lexicographic order, the change of basis matrix is triangular.

                At a point $\tilde{a} + b \in X_d^{\tilde{a}}$, we have
                \[B_{a}^{\tilde{a}} (\tilde{a} + b) = \binom{b}{a}.\]
                In particular, $B_{a}^{\tilde{a}} (\tilde{a} + b) = 0$ unless $a \leq b$ and $B_{a}^{\tilde{a}} (\tilde{a} + a) = 1$.
                This implies that the vectors $\operatorname{ev}_d^{\tilde{a}} (B_{a}^{\tilde{a}} (x))$ are linearly independent, and hence $\operatorname{ev}_d^{\tilde{a}}$ is injective.
                Both the domain and codomain have dimension $\binom{n+d}{n}$, and so, $\operatorname{ev}_d^{\tilde{a}}$ is in fact an isomorphism.

                To verify \eqref{eq:interpolation_1}, we evaluate the right-hand side at $\tilde{a} + c$. This gives
                \begin{align*}
                        \left( \sum_{a \in L_d} b_{a}^{\tilde{a}} (\mu) B_{a}^{\tilde{a}} \right) (\tilde{a} + c) &= \sum_{a \in L_d} b_{a}^{\tilde{a}} (\mu) B_{a}^{\tilde{a}} (\tilde{a} + c) \\
                        &= \sum_{a \in L_d} b_{a}^{\tilde{a}} (\mu) \binom{c}{a} \\ 
                        &= \sum_{b \leq a \leq c}  (-1)^{\lvert a \rvert - \lvert b \rvert} \binom{c}{a} \binom{a}{b} \mu (\tilde{a} + b) \\
                        &= \sum_{b \leq a \leq c}  (-1)^{\lvert a \rvert - \lvert b \rvert} \binom{c}{b} \binom{c - b}{a - b} \mu (\tilde{a} + b).
                \end{align*}
                For a fixed $b$, we set $e = a - b$. The condition on the sum becomes $0 \leq e \leq c - b$ and $\lvert e \rvert = \lvert a \rvert - \lvert b \rvert$.
                Therefore, we have that 
                \begin{equation}\label{eq:interpolation_2}
                        \sum_{b \leq a \leq c}  (-1)^{\lvert a \rvert - \lvert b \rvert} \binom{c}{b} \binom{c - b}{a - b} \mu (\tilde{a} + b) = \sum_{b \leq c} \mu ( \tilde{a} + b) \binom{c}{b} \sum_{e \leq c - b} (-1)^{\lvert e \rvert} \binom{c - b}{e} 
                \end{equation}
                The inner sum on the right-hand side of \eqref{eq:interpolation_2} can be computed by a multi-index version of the binomial theorem. 
                Namely, it vanishes unless $b = c$ in which case it is 1. Therefore,
                \[\sum_{b \leq c} \mu ( \tilde{a} + b) \binom{c}{b} \sum_{e \leq c - b} (-1)^{\lvert e \rvert} \binom{c - b}{e} = \mu (\tilde{a} + c).\]

label: cor:homog_interpolation
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:homog_interpolation}\footnote{Corollary \ref{cor:homog_interpolation} was discovered by ChatGPT without proof in the case of $n=2$ 
                and $\tilde{a} = ( 2,4)$ when it attempted to improve upon Algorithm \ref{algo:coeff_algo}. 
                The author believes that ChatGPT's discovery was based on earlier work of Dyn--Floater \cite{DF}; although, ChatGPT did not provide any references, so this is mostly speculation. }
                Let $\tilde{a} \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^n$.
                \begin{enumerate}
                        \item There is an isomorphism of vector spaces
                        \[\operatorname{ev}_d^{\tilde{a}} : A_{n+1}^d \stackrel{\sim}{\to} \operatorname{Fun} (Y_d^{\tilde{a}}, \mathbbm{k}), \qquad p \mapsto (a \mapsto p(a)).\]
                        \item For a function $\mu : Y_d^{\tilde{a}} \to \mathbbm{k}$, we set
                        \[\overline{b}_{a}^{\tilde{a}} (\mu) = \sum_{b \leq a} (-1)^{\lvert a \rvert - \lvert b \rvert} \binom{a}{b} \mu (\tilde{a} + b, 1).\]
                        Then 
                        \[(\operatorname{ev}_d^{\tilde{a}})^{-1} (\mu) (x_1, \ldots, x_{n+1}) = \sum_{a \in L_d} \overline{b}_{a}^{\tilde{a}} (\mu) x_{n+1}^d B_{a}^{\tilde{a}} \left( \frac{x_1}{x_{n+1}}, \ldots, \frac{x_n}{x_{n+1}} \right).\]
                \end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By construction the following diagram commutes,
                \[\begin{tikzcd}
A_{n+1}^d \arrow[d, "\operatorname{ev}_d^{\tilde{a}}"'] \arrow[r, "\sim"] & A_n^{\leq d} \arrow[d, "\operatorname{ev}_d^{\tilde{a}}"] \\
{\operatorname{Fun} (Y_d^{\tilde{a}}, \mathbbm{k})} \arrow[r, "\sim"]              & {\operatorname{Fun} (X_d^{\tilde{a}}, \mathbbm{k}),}               
\end{tikzcd}\]
where the top horizontal map is given by dehomogenization and the bottom horizontal map is induced from the set-theoretic bijection $X_d^{\tilde{a}} \to Y_d^{\tilde{a}}$ taking $a$ to $(a, 1)$.
The corollary then follows from translating the statement of Proposition~\ref{prop:interpolation} along this commutative diagram.

title: Remark

                The advantage of Corollary~\ref{cor:homog_interpolation} is that for $d < d'$, the points we need to evaluate a polynomial at satisfy $Y_{d}^{\tilde{a}} \subset Y_{d'}^{\tilde{a}}$.

title: Definition
body_md: We say that $\tilde{a} \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{r-1}$ is $K$-\emph{regular} if $\alpha (a) \neq 0$ for all $\alpha \in \Phi$ and $a \in Y_K^{\tilde{a}}$.
head: environment

label: lem:existence_of_K_regular
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:existence_of_K_regular}
                Assume that $\Phi$ is finite. There exists some $\tilde{a} = (\tilde{a}_1, \ldots, \tilde{a}_{r-1}) \in \mathbb{Z}_{> 0}^{r-1}$ such that $\tilde{a}$ is $K$-regular.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The case of $r=1$ is obvious. Assume that $r \geq 2$. Let $\alpha \in \Phi$ and $a = (a_1, \ldots, a_{r-1}) \in L_K$.
                Write
                \[\alpha = \sum_{i=1}^r b_i x_i.\]
                for some $b_i \in \mathbbm{k}$. 
                We will evaluate $\alpha$ at the point $(t + a_1,t^2 + a_2, \ldots, t^{r-1} + a_{r-1}, 1)$ where $t$ is a formal variable,
                \[p_{\alpha, a} (t) \coloneq \alpha (t + a_1,t^2 + a_2, \ldots, t^{r-1} + a_{r-1}, 1) = b_r + \sum_{i=1}^{r-1} b_i a_i + \sum_{i=1}^{r-1} b_i t^i \in \mathbbm{k} [t].\]
                Note that $p_{\alpha, a} \neq 0$. Indeed, if some $b_i \neq 0$ with $i < r$, it has a nonzero positive-degree coefficient.
                Otherwise, it is the nonzero constant $b_r$.
                
                Note that $p_{\alpha, a}$ has finitely many roots.
                Since $\Phi$ and $L_K$ are finite, the union of the roots of $p_{\alpha, a}$ for all $\alpha \in \Phi$ and $a \in L_K$ is also finite.
                In particular, there must be some positive integer $T$ which is not a root of $p_{\alpha, a}$. We set   
                \[\tilde{a} = (T, T^2, \ldots, T^{r-1}).\]
                This choice of $\tilde{a}$ is $K$-regular.

label: ex:K_reg
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:K_reg}
                \begin{enumerate}
                        \item   Let $(W,S)$ be any Coxeter system of finite rank. Let $\mathfrak{h}^* = \bigoplus_{s \in S} \mathbb{R} \alpha_s$.
                                Define elements $\alpha_s^{\vee} \in \mathfrak{h} = (\mathfrak{h}^*)^*$ by
                                \[\langle \alpha_t^{\vee}, \alpha_s \rangle = -2\cos(\pi/m_{st}),\]
                                where we set $m_{ss} = 1$ and $\pi/\infty = 0$ by convention. The realization $\mathfrak{h}$ is called the \emph{dual geometric realization}.
                                By \cite[Theorem 5.4]{Humphreys}, any root $\alpha \in \Phi$ can be written as
                                \[\alpha = \sum_{s} c_s \alpha_s\]
                                with all $c_s \geq 0$ or all $c_s \leq 0$, with at least one nonzero coefficient.
                                Every point on $Y_K^{(1,\ldots, 1)}$ has strictly positive coordinates with respect to the simple-root basis. Since every root has either all positive or all negative coefficients, it evaluates non-trivially at every such point.
                                Therefore, the shift $\tilde{a} = (1,\ldots, 1) \in \mathbb{Z}_{ > 0}^{r-1}$ is $K$ regular for every $K \geq 0$.
                        \item   Let $W = H_3$ and $\mathfrak{h}$ be the golden realization. The set of simple roots forms a basis for $\mathfrak{h}^*$.
                                There are 30 roots listed below.
                                \[
                                \begin{matrix}
                                        \alpha_s & \alpha_t & \alpha_u \\
                                         -\alpha_s & -\alpha_t & -\alpha_u \\
                                        \alpha_t + \alpha_u & \alpha_s + \phi \alpha_t & \phi \alpha_s + \alpha_t \\ 
                                        -\alpha_t - \alpha_u & -\alpha_s - \phi \alpha_t & -\phi \alpha_s - \alpha_t \\
                                        \phi (\alpha_s + \alpha_t) & \phi \alpha_s + \alpha_t + \alpha_u & \alpha_s + \phi (\alpha_t + \alpha_u) \\
                                         - \phi(\alpha_s + \alpha_t) & -\phi \alpha_s - \alpha_t - \alpha_u & -\alpha_s - \phi ( \alpha_t + \alpha_u) \\
                                        \phi (\alpha_s + \alpha_t + \alpha_u) & \phi (\alpha_s + \alpha_t) + (\alpha_t + \alpha_u) &  \phi (\alpha_s + \alpha_t + \alpha_u) + \alpha_t \\
                                         -\phi (\alpha_s + \alpha_t + \alpha_u) & -\phi (\alpha_s + \alpha_t) - (\alpha_t + \alpha_u) & -\phi (\alpha_s + \alpha_t + \alpha_u) - \alpha_t \\
                                         \phi (\alpha_s + \alpha_t) + (\alpha_s + \alpha_t + \alpha_u) & \phi (\alpha_s + \alpha_t + \alpha_u) + (\alpha_s + \alpha_t) & \phi (\alpha_s + 2 \alpha_t + \alpha_u) +  \alpha_s \\
                                         -\phi (\alpha_s + \alpha_t) - (\alpha_s + \alpha_t + \alpha_u) & -\phi (\alpha_s + \alpha_t + \alpha_u) - (\alpha_s + \alpha_t) & -\phi (\alpha_s + 2 \alpha_t + \alpha_u) -  \alpha_s 
                                \end{matrix}
                                \] 
                                Every root in this list has either positive or negative coefficients under the embedding $\phi = (1 + \sqrt{5})/2 > 0$. The same argument as in (1) shows that the shift $\tilde{a} = (1,1)$ is $K$-regular for every $K \geq 0$.
                        \item Let $W = I_2 (\infty)$ with $\mathfrak{h}^* = \mathbb{Q} e_1 \oplus \mathbb{Q} e_2$ and set $\alpha_s = e_1$ and $\alpha_t = e_2 - e_1$.
                        We can make $\mathfrak{h} = (\mathfrak{h}^*)^*$ into a realization with Cartan matrix
                        \[\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\]
                        Every sum of the form $e_1 + ne_2$ for $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ is a root for $\mathfrak{h}$.
                        At every point $(a,1)$ with integer $a$, the root $e_1 - ae_2$ vanishes. In particular, $a \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ is never $K$-regular.
                        \end{enumerate}

\label{prop:eq_testing_interpolate}
                Assume that $\Phi$ is finite.
                Let $\varphi, \psi : B_{\underline{x}} \to B_{\underline{y}}$ be two morphisms of degree $d$.
                Enumerate the admissible double leaves from $B_{\underline{x}}$ to $B_{\underline{y}}$ by $\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_1, \ldots, \mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_{N_d}$ as in Algorithm~\ref{algo:coeff_algo_interpolate}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $\varphi - \psi = \sum_i c_i \mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_i$ where $c_i \in R^{2k_i}$.
                Suppose inductively that $c_j = 0$ for $j < i$. Theorem~\ref{thm:lower_triang_of_coord_functionals} gives
                \[\lambda_i (\varphi - \psi) = c_i \lambda_i (\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_i).\]
                By assumption, $\lambda_i (\varphi - \psi) (a) = 0$ and $\lambda_i (\mathbb{L}\mathbb{L}_i) (a) \neq 0$ for all $a \in Y_{k_i}^{\tilde{a}}$.
                As a result, $c_i (a) = 0$ for all $a \in Y_{k_i}^{\tilde{a}}$. Corollary~\ref{cor:homog_interpolation} then gives that $c_i = 0$. The converse is immediate.

title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:integral_models}
                Every balanced realization admits an integral model.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\mathfrak{h}$ be a balanced realization of $(W,S)$ over $\mathbbm{k}$ with Cartan matrix $(a_{st})$. 

                Let $s,t \in S$ with $s \neq t$ and write $m = m_{st}$.
                We define a ring associated to the unordered pair $\{s,t\}$,
                \[A_{\{s,t\}} \coloneq \begin{cases} \mathbb{Z}[x_{st}, x_{ts}] / (x_{st}, x_{ts}) & m = 2, \\ \mathbb{Z} [x_{st}, x_{ts}]/(\Psi_m' (x_{st}), x_{st} - x_{ts}) & m > 2 \text{ odd}, \\ \mathbb{Z} [x_{st}, x_{ts}] / (\Psi_m (x_{st} x_{ts})) & m > 2 \text{ even}, \\ \mathbb{Z} [x_{st}, x_{ts}] & m=\infty. \end{cases}\]
                Here $\Psi_m$ and $\Psi_m'$ are the minimal polynomials from \eqref{eq:min_polys}.
                We then define a ring
                \[A \coloneq \bigotimes_{\{s,t\} \subset S} A_{\{s,t\}}.\]
                Each factor is free as a $\mathbb{Z}$-module. In the odd case, this follows from division by the monic polynomial $\Psi_m'$. In the even case, writing $d = \deg \Psi_m$, the monomials $x_{st}^i x_{ts}^j$ with $\min (i,j) < d$ form a $\mathbb{Z}$-basis of the quotient. Division by the leading monomial $x_{st}^d x_{ts}^d$ gives existence and uniqueness of the remainder. Hence $A$ is free over $\mathbb{Z}$.
                Define a Cartan matrix $(\tilde{a}_{st})$ associated to $A$ given by $\tilde{a}_{ss} = 2$ for all $s \in S$ and $\tilde{a}_{st} = -x_{st}$ for $s \neq t$.
                By Theorem~\ref{thm:abe_conditions}, there exists a ring homomorphism 
                \begin{equation}\label{eq:integral_models_1}
                  A \to \mathbbm{k}, \qquad x_{st} \mapsto -a_{st}.      
                \end{equation}

                Fix $\delta_s \in \mathfrak{h}^*$ for each $s \in S$ such that $\langle \alpha_s^{\vee}, \delta_s \rangle = 1$.
                We can define 
                \[\overline{A} = A [d_{st} : s\neq t \in S].\]
                By convention, we set $d_{ss} = 1$. We can now extend \eqref{eq:integral_models_1} to a morphism
                \[\tau : \overline{A} \to \mathbbm{k}, \qquad d_{st} \mapsto \langle \alpha_s^{\vee}, \delta_t \rangle.\]
                Of course, $\overline{A}$ is still a free $\mathbb{Z}$-module. We define a prime ideal $\mathfrak{q} = \ker (\tau)$.
                Let $\mathfrak{p} \subseteq \mathfrak{q}$ be a minimal prime ideal and define
                \[\mathcal{Z} = \overline{A}/\mathfrak{p}.\]
                The ring homomorphism $\tau$ factors through a ring homomorphism
                \[\sigma : \mathcal{Z} \to \mathbbm{k}.\]
                Note that since $\mathfrak{p}$ is a minimal prime ideal and $\overline{A}$ is free over $\mathbb{Z}$, we must have that $\mathcal{Z}$ has characteristic $0$.

                Define a free $\mathcal{Z}$-module,
                \[\mathfrak{h}_{\mathcal{Z}}^* \coloneq \bigoplus_{s \in S} \mathcal{Z} \alpha_s \oplus \bigoplus_{t \in S} \mathcal{Z} e_t.\]
                We define the coroots in $\mathfrak{h}_{\mathcal{Z}} \coloneq (\mathfrak{h}_{\mathcal{Z}}^*)^*$ by
                \[\langle \alpha_s^{\vee}, \alpha_t \rangle = \tilde{a}_{st} \qquad\text{and}\qquad \langle \alpha_s^{\vee}, e_t \rangle = d_{st}.\]
                The Cartan entries satisfy the minimal-polynomial conditions of \cite[Definition 1.1]{Hazi2}. By \cite[Proposition 1.4]{Hazi2}, the reflection formulas define a $W$-action on $\mathfrak{h}_{\mathcal{Z}}^*$, and dually on $\mathfrak{h}_{\mathcal{Z}}$. 

                Next, we can verify that Demazure surjectivity holds for $\mathfrak{h}_{\mathcal{Z}}$.
                By definition, each $\alpha_s$ is a basis vector of $\mathfrak{h}_{\mathcal{Z}}^*$, so $\alpha_s : \mathfrak{h}_{\mathcal{Z}} \to \mathcal{Z}$ is surjective.
                On the other hand, $\alpha_s^{\vee} (e_s) = d_{ss} = 1$, and so $\alpha_s^{\vee} : \mathfrak{h}_{\mathcal{Z}}^* \to \mathcal{Z}$ is also surjective.
                Abe's conditions \eqref{eq:qbinom_vanishing} and the balancedness equations \eqref{eq:balanced} are satisfied by our construction using Theorem~\ref{thm:abe_conditions}.
                Therefore, $\mathfrak{h}_{\mathcal{Z}}$ is a balanced realization of $(W,S)$ over $\mathcal{Z}$.

                Finally, we define $f : \mathfrak{h}_{\mathcal{Z}}^* \to \mathfrak{h}^*$ by $\alpha_s \mapsto \alpha_s$ and $e_t \mapsto \delta_t$. 
                The pair $(\sigma, f)$ then defines a morphism of realizations $\mathfrak{h}_{\mathcal{Z}} \to \mathfrak{h}$ which completes the proof.

title: Lemma
head: environment

label: eq:universal_H3_realization
title: Proof
body_md:
Consider the Cartan matrix of an arbitrary balanced realization $\mathfrak{h}$ over an integral domain $\mathbbm{k}$,
                \[\begin{bmatrix}
                        a_{ss} & a_{st} & a_{su} \\
                        a_{ts} & a_{tt} & a_{tu} \\
                        a_{us} & a_{ut} & a_{uu} 
                \end{bmatrix}.\]
                We must have that $a_{ss} = a_{tt} = a_{uu} = 2$ by the definition of a realization.
                For the entries $a_{su}$ and $a_{us}$, the vanishing of quantum binomial coefficients forces
                \[-a_{su} = [2]_x (-a_{su}, -a_{us}) = 0 \qquad\text{and}\qquad -a_{us} = [2]_y (-a_{su}, -a_{us}) = 0.\]
                As a result, $a_{su} = a_{us} = 0$.
                Next, for the entries $a_{tu}$ and $a_{ut}$, balancedness forces
                \[ -a_{tu} = [2]_x (-a_{tu}, -a_{ut}) = 1 \qquad\text{and}\qquad -a_{ut} = [2]_y (-a_{tu}, -a_{ut}) = 1.\]
                As a result, $a_{tu} = a_{ut} = -1$.  Finally, for the entries $a_{st}$ and $a_{ts}$, balancedness forces
                \[[2]_x (-a_{st}, -a_{ts}) = [3]_x (-a_{st}, a_{ts}) = [3]_y (-a_{st}, a_{ts}) = [2]_y (-a_{st}, -a_{ts}).\]
                Evaluating these quantum numbers gives $\theta \coloneq -a_{st} = -a_{ts}$ and $\theta^2 - \theta - 1 = 0$.
                The Cartan matrix then is of the form
                \begin{equation}\label{eq:universal_H3_realization}
                \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -\theta & 0 \\ - \theta & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}.
                \end{equation}

                Set $\mathcal{Z} = \mathbb{Z} [\tau]/(\tau^2 - \tau - 1)$. We can then define a realization
                \[\mathfrak{h}_{\mathcal{Z}}^* \coloneq \mathcal{Z} \alpha_s \oplus \mathcal{Z} \alpha_t \oplus \mathcal{Z} \alpha_u.\]
                We define $\alpha_r^{\vee} \in \mathfrak{h}_{\mathcal{Z}} \coloneq (\mathfrak{h}_{\mathcal{Z}}^*)^*$ for $r=s,t,u$ by the Cartan matrix \eqref{eq:universal_H3_realization} where $\theta = \tau$.
                It is a tad tedious, but not difficult to check that $\mathfrak{h}_{\mathcal{Z}}$ is a balanced realization of $W$.

                We can then define a morphism of realizations $\mathfrak{h}_{\mathcal{Z}} \to \mathfrak{h}$ as follows. The ring homomorphism $\mathcal{Z} \to \mathbbm{k}$ is defined by $\tau \mapsto \theta$.
                The linear map $\mathfrak{h}_{\mathcal{Z}}^* \to \mathfrak{h}^*$ is defined by $\alpha_r \mapsto \alpha_r$ for $r\in S$. The Cartan matrix \eqref{eq:universal_H3_realization} 
                guarantees that this data defines a morphism of realizations. 
                
                Finally, the map $\mathcal{Z} = \mathbb{Z} [\tau]/(\tau^2 - \tau - 1) \to \mathbb{Q} (\phi)$ defined by $\tau \mapsto \phi$ induces an isomorphism $\operatorname{Frac} (\mathcal{Z}) \cong \mathbb{Q} (\phi)$.
                Over $\mathbb{Q} (\phi)$ the Cartan matrix has determinant $2 (2 - \phi) \neq 0$. Thus the simple roots in the golden realization form a basis. Sending our three basis roots to those roots gives an isomorphism between the base change of $\mathfrak{h}_{\mathcal{Z}}$ to $\mathbb{Q} (\phi)$ and the golden realization.

label: lem:gen_bs_ass_satisfied_for_H3
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Recall that there exists some $\theta \in \mathbbm{k}^{\times}$ such that the Cartan matrix is of the form \eqref{eq:universal_H3_realization}.
                The following table describes the action of each simple reflection on the simple roots,
                \begin{center}
                        \begin{tabular}{c | c | c | c}
                            & $\alpha_s$ & $\alpha_t$ & $\alpha_u$ \\
                            \hline
                            $s$ & $-\alpha_s$ & $\alpha_t + \theta \alpha_s$ & $\alpha_u$ \\
                            \hline
                            $t$ & $\alpha_s + \theta \alpha_t$ & $-\alpha_t$ & $\alpha_t + \alpha_u$ \\
                            \hline
                            $u$ & $\alpha_s$ & $\alpha_t + \alpha_u$ & $-\alpha_u$    
                        \end{tabular}
                \end{center}
                We first claim that $W_I \to \operatorname{Aut} (\mathfrak{h}^*)$ is injective. First, we can calculate using the above table that $st (\alpha_u) - \alpha_u = \alpha_t + \theta \alpha_s$.
                Note that $\alpha_t + \theta \alpha_s \neq 0$ since $\langle \alpha_u^{\vee}, \alpha_t + \theta \alpha_u \rangle = -1$, and hence $st (\alpha_u) \neq \alpha_u$. Therefore, $st$ acts non-trivially on $\mathfrak{h}^*$.
                Moreover, since $st$ has prime order $3$, $\langle st \rangle$ has index $2$ in $W_I$, we must have that the kernel of $W_I \to \operatorname{Aut} (\mathfrak{h}^*)$ is contained in the center of $W_I$.
                However, a dihedral group of the form $D_{2p}$ for an odd prime $p$ has trivial center, therefore, the kernel must be trivial.

                Next, we claim that $W_J \to \operatorname{Aut} (\mathfrak{h}^*)$ is injective. 
                Again, we can calculate using the above table to get that $tu (\alpha_s) - \alpha_s = \theta \alpha_t$. Since $\langle \alpha_u^{\vee}, \theta \alpha_t \rangle = - \theta \neq 0$, we have that $tu (\alpha_s) \neq \alpha_s$.
                Again since $tu$ has odd prime order $3$, the same argument as for $W_I$ shows that $W_J \to \operatorname{Aut} (\mathfrak{h}^*)$ is injective.

                It is easy to check from the definitions that
                \[\partial_I (\alpha_t \alpha_u^4) = -\theta^3 \qquad\text{and}\qquad \partial_J (\alpha_s^2 \alpha_t) = -\theta^2.\]
                Now, $\theta$ satisfies $\theta^2 - \theta - \theta = 0$, so we can check that $-\theta^{-3} = 3-2\theta$ and $-\theta^{-2} = \theta - 2$.
                The claim then readily follows.

title: Proof
body_md:
We can compute,
                \begin{align*}
                        \langle \iota_{\underline{w}} (f \otimes g) , \iota_{\underline{w}} (f' \otimes g') \rangle_{\underline{w}} &= (\partial_{s_k} \ldots \partial_{s_1}) (ff') gg' \\
                        &= \partial_I (ff') gg' \\
                        &= \langle f \otimes g, f' \otimes g' \rangle_I.
                \end{align*}
                The pairing on the left is the canonical perfect pairing on $B_{\underline{w}}$ given by \eqref{eq:pairing}. The second equality uses the fact that $w_I^{-1} = w_I$ and the well-definedness of $\partial_I$.
                Adjointness and nondegeneracy now give that $p_{\underline{w}} \iota_{\underline{w}} = \operatorname{id}_{B_I}$ as desired. The idempotence and self-adjointness of $e_{\underline{w}}$ immediately follow.

title: Lemma

label: eq:thick_relns_1
title: Proof
body_md:
The first relation means that $p_{\underline{w}} \iota_{\underline{w}} = \operatorname{id}_{B_I}$ which is proved in Lemma~\ref{lem:gen_proj}.

                For the second relation, we write $\underline{w} = \underline{x} s$ for some $s$ corresponding to the red strand. The relation can be translated algebraically to mean
                \begin{equation}\label{eq:thick_relns_1}
                        (p_{\underline{w}} \otimes \operatorname{id}_{B_s}) (\operatorname{id}_{B_{\underline{x}}} \otimes \nu^s) \iota_{\underline{w}} = \nu^{I, s}.
                \end{equation}
                It is easy to check from the definitions that
                \[(\operatorname{id}_{B_{\underline{x}}} \otimes \nu^s) \iota_{\underline{w}} = (\iota_{\underline{w}} \otimes \operatorname{id}_{B_s}) \nu^{I, s}.\]
                We can then compose with $p_{\underline{w}} \otimes \operatorname{id}_{B_s}$ and use the first relation to deduce,
                \[ (p_{\underline{w}} \otimes \operatorname{id}_{B_s}) (\operatorname{id}_{B_{\underline{x}}} \otimes \nu^s) \iota_{\underline{w}} = (p_{\underline{w}} \otimes \operatorname{id}_{B_s}) (\iota_{\underline{w}} \otimes \operatorname{id}_{B_s}) \nu^{I, s} = \nu^{I,s}. \]

                The third relation follows from the second by duality.

                The fourth relation is an easy consequence of the first three.

                For the fifth relation, we first define a map $A_{\underline{w}} : B_I \to B_I \otimes_R B_{\underline{w}}$ as the map on the right-hand side. 
                In more detail, we can define this map recursively. Set $A_{\varnothing} = \operatorname{id}_{B_I}$, and then
                \[A_{\underline{x} s} = (A_{\underline{x}} \otimes \operatorname{id}_{B_s}) \nu^{I, s} .\]
                By induction, we have that 
                \[A_{\underline{w}} (f \otimes g) = f \otimes 1 \otimes \ldots \otimes 1 \otimes g = (\operatorname{id}_{B_I} \otimes \iota_{\underline{w}}) \nu^I (f \otimes g).\]
                Note that $(\operatorname{id}_{B_I} \otimes \iota_{\underline{w}}) \nu^I$ is the left-hand side of the relation. 

                Finally, the sixth relation follows from the fifth by duality.

The relation can be found in \cite[(6.17)]{Elib}. 
                It is equivalent to the algebraic relation,
                \[\iota_{{}_s \underline{m}} p_{{}_s \underline{m}} = \beta_{ts} \beta_{st}.\]
                We will prove this by showing that
                \begin{equation}\label{eq:thick_jw_1}
                        \beta_{st} =  \iota_{{}_t \underline{m}} p_{{}_s \underline{m}}. 
                \end{equation}
                To see why this is sufficient, we can apply Lemma~\ref{lem:gen_proj} (1) to get
                \[ \iota_{{}_s \underline{m}} p_{{}_s \underline{m}}  =  \iota_{{}_s \underline{m}} p_{{}_t \underline{m}} \iota_{{}_t \underline{m}} p_{{}_s \underline{m}}  \stackrel{\eqref{eq:thick_jw_1}}{=} \beta_{ts} \beta_{st} .  \]

                The morphism $\beta_{st}$ is uniquely characterized in taking the $1$-tensor to the $1$-tensor. 
                It is easy to see from the definitions that $\iota_{{}_s \underline{m}} p_{{}_t \underline{m}}$ also takes the 1-tensor to the 1-tensor. Therefore, \eqref{eq:thick_jw_1} holds.
